pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: What classes of bugs does continuous integration catch that testing on your own machine before a release does not? Why does running checks at merge time beat a manual pre-release test pass?
expected_points: works-on-my-machine bugs: uncommitted files, locally installed tools, local environment leaking in — the fresh machine has none of it
combination breakage between changes that are each fine alone
humans skip checks under pressure; the machine runs every check on every push
feedback distance: a bug caught minutes after its push is easy to place, weeks later it hides among hundreds of commits

questions.prompt: Walk me through your workflow file: what do `on:`, `jobs:`, `runs-on:`, and `steps:` each declare, and what is the difference between a `uses:` step and a `run:` step?
expected_points: on: lists the triggers — push and pull_request cover the CI contract
each job gets a fresh machine named by runs-on:
steps run in order; a non-zero exit code fails the run
uses: invokes a published reusable action (checkout clones the repo, setup-go installs the toolchain); run: executes a shell command

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment.
expected_points: integration: every push and merge request is built and tested automatically — output is a red/green verdict
delivery: every green main build is packaged and could be released; a human decides when
deployment: every green main build ships to production automatically — the tests are the release decision
it is a trust ladder: each level requires believing the one below

questions.prompt: What makes a workflow step a quality gate, and why did your gofmt gate need the `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"` idiom while `go vet ./...` could stand alone?
expected_points: a gate is a step whose non-zero exit code fails the run — exit codes are the whole contract
gofmt -l always exits 0 even when it lists offenders, so bare it can never fail
test -z exits non-zero when the output is non-empty, turning findings into a red step
go vet already exits non-zero on findings

questions.prompt: A pipeline run just went red. Describe your first moves, and what it means if you cannot reproduce the failure locally.
expected_points: open the failing step's log, not the summary; find the first error
reproduce by running that step's exact command locally
reproduces: ordinary debugging of your code; does not: an environment difference — uncommitted file, version mismatch, local-only state
fix the underlying cause — never delete the test or skip the step to go green

questions.prompt: Why does the runner start from an empty machine and clone your repo with actions/checkout, instead of reusing a machine that already has everything set up?
expected_points: the empty machine proves the repository is self-contained — everything needed is declared or committed
a reused machine accumulates state, hiding works-on-my-machine bugs and making runs non-reproducible

questions.prompt: You put the gofmt and vet gates before the tests. What is the argument for that order, and when might you run gates in parallel jobs instead?
expected_points: cheapest feedback first: a three-second formatting complaint should not wait on the whole test suite
parallel jobs trade machine time for wall-clock time — worth it once suites are slow enough that developers wait on them
